fetched_contents.text: The effects of oxidative stress on female reproduction: a review Abstract Oxidative stress (OS), a state characterized by an imbalance between pro-oxidant molecules including reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and antioxidant defenses, has been identified to play a key role in the pathogenesis of subfertility in both males and females. The adverse effects of OS on sperm quality and functions have been well documented. In females, on the other hand, the impact of OS on oocytes and reproductive functions remains unclear. This imbalance between pro-oxidants and antioxidants can lead to a number of reproductive diseases such as endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), and unexplained infertility. Pregnancy complications such as spontaneous abortion, recurrent pregnancy loss, and preeclampsia, can also develop in response to OS. Studies have shown that extremes of body weight and lifestyle factors such as cigarette smoking, alcohol use, and recreational drug use can promote excess free radical production, which could affect fertility. Exposures to environmental pollutants are of increasing concern, as they too have been found to trigger oxidative states, possibly contributing to female infertility. This article will review the currently available literature on the roles of reactive species and OS in both normal and abnormal reproductive physiological processes. Antioxidant supplementation may be effective in controlling the production of ROS and continues to be explored as a potential strategy to overcome reproductive disorders associated with infertility. However, investigations conducted to date have been through animal or in vitro studies, which have produced largely conflicting results. The impact of OS on assisted reproductive techniques (ART) will be addressed, in addition to the possible benefits of antioxidant supplementation of ART culture media to increase the likelihood for ART success. Future randomized controlled clinical trials on humans are necessary to elucidate the precise mechanisms through which OS affects female reproductive abilities, and will facilitate further explorations of the possible benefits of antioxidants to treat infertility. The pathogenesis of ovarian aging is complex and diverse; oxidative stress (OS) is considered to be a key factor. This review focuses on the fact that OS status accelerates the ovarian aging process by promoting apoptosis, inflammation, mitochondrial damage, telomere shortening and biomacromolecular damage. Current evidence suggests that aging, smoking, high-sugar diets, pressure, superovulation, chemotherapeutic agents and industrial pollutants can be factors that accelerate ovarian aging by exacerbating OS status. In addition, we review the role of nuclear factor E2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), Sirtuin (Sirt), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), protein kinase B (AKT), Forkhead box O (FoxO) and Klotho signaling pathways during the process of ovarian aging. We also explore the role of antioxidant therapies such as melatonin, vitamins, stem cell therapies, antioxidant monomers and Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), and investigate the roles of these supplements with respect to the reduction of OS and the improvement of ovarian function. This review provides a rationale for antioxidant therapy to improve ovarian aging. Keywords: Ovarian aging, Oxidative stress, Antioxidant, Apoptosis, Inflammation, Cigarette smoking, Melatonin, Vitamin C, Nuclear factor E2-related factor 2 Introduction Aging is an irreversible physiological and pathological phenomenon in normal metabolism [1]. Aging is complex and multiple factors are known to contribute towards the overall aging process and phenotype [2]. In the female body, the ovary acts as a natural biological clock, thus controlling the process of aging [3]. Ovarian aging refers to the process of gradual decline and eventual exhaustion of ovarian function. Two major categories of ovarian aging have been identified: physiological and pathological. Physiological ovarian aging refers to the process by which ovarian function deteriorates naturally with age until menopause. Pathological ovarian aging refers to the premature decline of ovarian function, including diminished ovarian reserve (DOR), premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), and poor ovarian response (POR) in the field of in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer (IVF-ET). Pathological aging can be caused by a variety of pathogenic factors [4]. Ovarian aging is characterized by menstrual disorders (amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea) and reduced reproductive function, accompanied by elevated levels of gonadotropins and decreased levels of estrogen. In terms of pathology, ovarian aging predominantly manifests as a reduction in the number of follicles and a decline in the quality of oocytes [5]. The terminal stage of ovarian aging is menopause. Following menopause, dysfunction of the endocrine, cardiovascular and nervous systems, among others, becomes apparent or aggravated with hormonal changes in female body. Therefore, ovarian aging is considered an important node in the process of female aging. As a classic theory of aging, free radical theory was first proposed in the 1950s. The important role of free radical has been extensively studied across multiple diseases and is considered a key mechanism of ovarian aging. Free radicals are a high-activity pro-oxidation group of molecules produced during aerobic metabolism, including reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) [6]. ROS is primarily a byproduct of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. A temperate amount of ROS is essential for the normal physiological functions of the body. ROS are not only involved in the synthesis of active substances, cellular detoxification and immune function [7], they also act as an important second messenger that participates in the intercellular signal transduction and regulation of gene expression, thereby maintaining cellular homeostasis [8]. Under physiological conditions, the oxidative and antioxidant systems are in dynamic equilibrium. The antioxidant system is composed of both enzymes and non-enzymes. Of these, the key enzymes include superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), glutathione (GSH) and glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px). Non-enzymes mainly include melatonin, vitamins (C, E) and trace elements (copper, zinc and selenium). However, when ROS are overproduced or antioxidant utilization increases, this leads to an imbalance of redox reactions and induces an oxidative stress (OS) state in the body [9]. Extensive studies have shown that the OS state of the ovarian microenvironment can result in pathological damage, including meiotic arrest in oocytes, granulosa cell apoptosis, and corpus luteum dysfunction, thus accelerating the process of ovarian aging. Supplementation with antioxidants can improve the ovarian OS state and enhance ovarian function. This article reviews research progress in the field of OS in relation to ovarian aging. The physiological role of ROS in the ovary In the ovary, ROS are involved in the regulation of oocyte growth, meiosis, ovulation and other physiological processes [10]. During follicular growth, increased steroid production leads to the expression of cytochrome P450, thus resulting in ROS formation. fetched_contents.text: Oxidative Stress and Placental Pathogenesis: A Contemporary Overview of Potential Biomarkers and Emerging Therapeutics Abstract Oxidative stress (OS) plays a crucial role in placental pathogenesis and pregnancy-related complications. This review explores OS’s impact on placental development and function, focusing on novel biomarkers for the early detection of at-risk pregnancies and emerging therapeutic strategies. We analyzed recent research on OS in placental pathophysiology, examining its sources, mechanisms, and effects. While trophoblast invasion under low-oxygen conditions and hypoxia-induced OS regulate physiological placental development, excessive OS can lead to complications like miscarriage, preeclampsia, and intrauterine growth restriction. Promising OS biomarkers, including malondialdehyde, 8-isoprostane, and the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio, show potential for the early detection of pregnancy complications. Therapeutic strategies targeting OS, such as mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, Nrf2 activators, and gasotransmitter therapies, demonstrate encouraging preclinical results. However, clinical translation remains challenging. Future research should focus on validating these biomarkers in large-scale studies and developing personalized therapies to modulate placental OS. Emerging approaches like extracellular vesicle-based therapies and nanomedicine warrant further investigation for both diagnostic and therapeutic applications in pregnancy-related complications. Integrating OS biomarkers with other molecular and cellular markers offers improved potential for the early identification of at-risk pregnancies. Introduction Pregnancy represents a unique physiological state characterized by complex adaptations that ensure the survival and growth of the developing fetus. Central to this process is the placenta, an organ that functions as the critical interface between the mother and fetus [1]. The placenta facilitates the exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste products; produces hormones essential for maintaining pregnancy; and modulates immune interactions to prevent fetal rejection [2]. The proper development and function of the placenta are therefore paramount for fetal health and successful pregnancy outcomes. A key factor influencing placental development and function is the delicate balance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) production and the antioxidant defense mechanisms that neutralize these reactive molecules [3]. ROS and RNS are generated as natural byproducts of cellular metabolism and play essential roles in cell signaling, gene expression, and defense against pathogens [4]. However, an imbalance favoring the accumulation of ROS/RNS leads to oxidative stress (OS), which can damage lipids, proteins, and DNA, disrupt cellular functions, and trigger cell death pathways such as apoptosis and autophagy [5]. In the placenta, OS is a double-edged sword. On one hand, controlled levels of ROS are necessary for normal placental functions, including trophoblast proliferation, differentiation, invasion, and angiogenesis [6]. These processes are crucial during early pregnancy when the placenta develops in a relatively low-oxygen environment [7]. Hypoxia, or low oxygen tension, stimulates the expression of hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1), a transcription factor that regulates genes involved in angiogenesis, metabolism, and cell survival [8]. HIF-1 activation under hypoxic conditions promotes the production of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), facilitating the formation of new blood vessels and ensuring adequate oxygen and nutrient supply to the developing fetus [9]. As pregnancy progresses, the placenta undergoes a transition from a hypoxic to a more oxygen-rich environment [10]. This shift is due to the remodeling of maternal spiral arteries by extravillous trophoblasts (EVTs), which replace the endothelial lining and transform the arteries into high-capacity, low-resistance vessels [11]. While the placenta has antioxidant systems to mitigate ROS-induced damage, excessive OS can overwhelm these defenses, leading to pathological conditions [13]. High levels of ROS can impair trophoblast function, inhibit EVT invasion, and disrupt spiral artery remodeling, resulting in reduced placental perfusion and nutrient exchange [14]. These events contribute to pregnancy complications such as preeclampsia (PE), characterized by hypertension and proteinuria, and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), where fetal growth is compromised [15]. These factors interfere with normal angiogenic signaling, further impairing placental function and contributing to maternal endothelial dysfunction [17]. Moreover, OS influences cellular processes such as autophagy and apoptosis in the placenta [19]. Evidence on how oxidative stress causes direct tissue damage in the female reproductive tract

Oxidative stress is most directly damaging to reproductive tissues where ROS generation is tightly coupled to physiological function and where antioxidant defenses are relatively limited or overwhelmed. The strongest evidence points to ovarian tissues, endometrium, and placental tissues as especially vulnerable. In the ovary, oxidative stress accelerates ovarian aging by promoting apoptosis, inflammation, mitochondrial damage, telomere shortening, and biomacromolecular damage [N2-F2]. This includes granulosa cell apoptosis, which is central to abnormal egg development and follicular atresia [N2-R2]. In the endometrium, oxidative stress is tied to decidualization and implantation, with evidence that resistance to oxidative stress is necessary for successful trophoblast invasion and tissue integrity [N3-R1]. Decidualization is also linked to endometrial receptivity, and dysregulation of this process can condition endometrial receptivity and contribute to pregnancy failure [N3-R2]. The placenta likewise shows that oxidative stress can be both physiological and pathological, with placental dysfunction and pregnancy complications such as miscarriage, preeclampsia, and intrauterine growth restriction arising from an imbalance between oxidants and antioxidants [N4-F3].

Reactive oxygen species alter cell signaling and DNA/RNA through multiple pathways. ROS can disrupt normal physiological signaling by acting as second messengers or by modifying signaling molecules. In the ovary, ROS are involved in the regulation of oocyte growth, meiosis, ovulation, and follicular development [N2-F2]. ROS also regulate meiotic arrest and recovery, while antioxidant control dominates the progression of meiosis II [N2-F2]. At the same time, ROS can damage DNA/RNA. The evidence explicitly states that oxidative stress can lead to DNA damage, and that 8-OHdG and other markers are used to measure DNA/RNA damage in oxidative stress contexts [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The broader review also notes that oxidative stress can trigger lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, DNA damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction [N1-R2]. In placental tissues, ROS/RNS can damage lipids, proteins, and DNA, disrupt cellular functions, and trigger apoptosis and autophagy [N4-F3]. These effects are not limited to direct DNA damage; ROS can also interfere with gene expression and signaling by modifying key proteins and metabolic pathways.

Inflammatory and fibrotic changes follow oxidative stress through a cascade of signaling and tissue responses. In the ovary, oxidative stress promotes apoptosis and inflammation, which together accelerate ovarian aging [N2-F2]. In the endometrium, oxidative stress is associated with altered decidualization and ER stress, which condition endometrial receptivity [N3-R2]. The placenta shows that oxidative stress can impair trophoblast function, inhibit EVT invasion, and disrupt spiral artery remodeling, leading to placental dysfunction and complications like preeclampsia and intrauterine growth restriction [N4-F3]. Inflammation is a central theme: ROS can drive inflammatory precursors, and oxidative stress can trigger cell death pathways such as apoptosis and autophagy [N4-F3]. Fibrotic-like changes are implied indirectly through tissue remodeling and loss of normal architecture, including granulosa cell loss and follicular atresia [N2-R2][N2-F2]. Taken together, oxidative stress does not merely cause localized DNA/RNA damage; it reshapes tissue homeostasis through inflammation, apoptosis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and remodeling [N1-R2][N2-F2][N4-F3].

Which tissues are most vulnerable? The ovarian follicle and granulosa cells are especially vulnerable because oxidative stress promotes apoptosis and follicular atresia [N2-R2][N2-F2]. The endometrium is vulnerable because decidualization and implantation are highly sensitive to oxidative stress and related signaling disturbances [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The placenta is vulnerable because oxidative stress can disrupt trophoblast invasion, spiral artery remodeling, and placental perfusion, with direct consequences for pregnancy outcomes [N4-F3]. These tissues share a common vulnerability: they are sites of active metabolism, differentiation, and immune/tissue remodeling, which make them especially sensitive to ROS overload and antioxidant deficiency [N1-R2][N2-F2][N4-F3].

Evidence on reproductive outcomes linked to oxidative stress

Oxidative stress is strongly linked to ovulatory dysfunction and anovulation through effects on ovarian function and follicle development. The ovarian aging review states that oxidative stress accelerates ovarian aging by promoting apoptosis, inflammation, mitochondrial damage, telomere shortening, and biomacromolecular damage [N2-F2]. It also notes that follicular fluid oxidative stress markers correlate with decreased embryo quality, and that oxidative stress contributes to the etiology of ovarian aging and other ovarian disorders [N2-R5]. In the ovary, oxidative stress impairs follicle development by promoting granulosa cell apoptosis and follicular atresia [N2-R2]. These effects are consistent with ovulatory dysfunction because they reduce follicle number and quality, disrupt steroid production, and compromise oocyte maturation [N2-F2]. The evidence also links oxidative stress to diminished ovarian reserve, premature ovarian insufficiency, and poor ovarian response, all of which are clinical manifestations of anovulation and reduced fertility [N2-F2]. In short, oxidative stress is not merely an incidental feature of ovarian aging; it is a driver of the structural and functional changes that underlie ovulatory failure [N2-F2][N2-R5].

Oxidative stress also plays a major role in early pregnancy loss and implantation failure. In the endometrium, oxidative stress affects decidualization and implantation receptivity. Dysregulation of the decidualization process due to ER stress and UPR conditions endometrial receptivity [N3-R2], and aberrant decidualization leads to pregnancy failures such as recurrent pregnancy loss and repeated implantation failure [N3-R3]. The placenta shows that oxidative stress contributes to both normal and abnormal placentation and is implicated in miscarriage, preeclampsia, and intrauterine growth restriction [N4-F3]. The placental review explicitly states that altered balance between oxidants and antioxidants can trigger oxidative stress in human placenta and has important implications in the etiology of recurrent pregnancy loss [N4-R4]. It also notes that oxidative stress biomarkers are strongly associated with disease progression and recurrent pregnancy loss [N4-R3]. These findings point to oxidative stress as a key contributor to early pregnancy failure by impairing implantation, decidualization, placental development, and trophoblast function [N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-F3][N4-R4].

As for biomarkers used to measure oxidative stress in reproductive health, the evidence supports a small set of well-established markers. ROS itself is proposed as a direct marker of oxidative stress [N6-R2][N6-R3]. 8-OHdG is proposed as a marker of DNA/RNA damage [N6-R2][N6-R3]. Malondialdehyde (MDA) is proposed as a marker of lipid peroxidation [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The placental review also highlights malondialdehyde, 8-isoprostane, and the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio as promising OS biomarkers [N4-F3]. The broader reproductive literature also notes that oxidative stress can be measured by lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, DNA damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction [N1-R2]. These markers are biologically relevant because they reflect different aspects of oxidative stress: ROS production, DNA/RNA damage, lipid damage, and inflammatory or vascular signaling [N6-R2][N6-R3][N4-F3]. However, the evidence also suggests that these markers are not interchangeable or universally applicable across tissues. In reproductive tissues, the placental review emphasizes that biomarker interpretation is context-dependent and that OS biomarkers can vary with disease state and measurement setting [N4-F3]. The human infertility literature similarly indicates that oxidative stress is associated with decreased fertility, but that the evidence is mostly derived from animal and in vitro studies, with limited direct human evidence [N5-R1].

Clinical and translational context for treating oxidative stress in female reproduction

Common antioxidant interventions and their reported effects on fertility are mostly indirect and mostly reported in non-human models. The ovarian aging review notes that antioxidant supplementation can improve the ovarian OS state and enhance ovarian function [N2-F2]. It also reviews antioxidant therapies such as melatonin, vitamins, stem cell therapies, antioxidant monomers, and Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), but the evidence base is largely experimental [N2-F2]. The broader oxidative stress review in female reproduction states that antioxidant supplementation may be effective in controlling ROS production and continues to be explored as a potential strategy to overcome reproductive disorders associated with infertility [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that antioxidant supplementation of ART culture media is of interest for improving ART success [N1-F1]. Taken together, the main reported effects are improved oxidative status and improved reproductive outcomes in experimental settings, but the evidence is not yet strong enough to establish definitive clinical efficacy [N2-F2][N1-F1].

Limitations and gaps in human evidence are substantial. The ovarian aging review explicitly states that investigations conducted to date have been through animal or in vitro studies, which have produced largely conflicting results [N2-F2]. The human female infertility review likewise notes that no studies to date have directly assessed the relationship in humans [N5-R1]. The oxidative stress review in female reproduction further emphasizes that future randomized controlled clinical trials on humans are necessary to elucidate the precise mechanisms through which OS affects female reproductive abilities [N1-F1]. These limitations suggest that human evidence remains weak, heterogeneous, and largely correlative [N5-R1][N1-F1].

How oxidative stress fits into broader reproductive disease mechanisms is important. The evidence shows that oxidative stress is not an isolated phenomenon but is embedded in the pathogenesis of several reproductive diseases and pregnancy complications. In the ovary, it is linked to ovarian aging, diminished ovarian reserve, premature ovarian insufficiency, poor ovarian response, PCOS, endometriosis, and unexplained infertility [N1-F1][N2-F2]. In the endometrium, it is linked to implantation failure and recurrent pregnancy loss [N3-R2][N3-R3]. In the placenta, it is linked to preeclampsia, intrauterine growth restriction, and miscarriage [N4-F3]. The broader reproductive literature also ties oxidative stress to lifestyle factors, environmental pollutants, obesity, malnutrition, cigarette smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs, and occupational exposures [N1-F1]. This places oxidative stress within a broader pathogenic framework in which reproductive dysfunction arises from metabolic, inflammatory, hormonal, and environmental insults that all contribute to ROS imbalance [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

Overall, the clinical and translational context is encouraging but cautious: antioxidants may improve reproductive outcomes in experimental models, but human evidence is still sparse, indirect, and conflicting. The major gap is the lack of large randomized trials in humans, and the major challenge is distinguishing true causal effects from confounding factors [N2-F2][N5-R1][N1-F1].

Evidence on biomarker interpretation and measurement limitations

Common oxidative stress biomarkers and their biological relevance are well supported in the evidence. ROS is proposed as a direct marker of oxidative stress [N6-R2][N6-R3]. 8-OHdG is proposed as a marker of DNA/RNA damage [N6-R2][N6-R3]. MDA is proposed as a marker of lipid peroxidation [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The placental review adds malondialdehyde, 8-isoprostane, and the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio as promising OS biomarkers [N4-F3]. The broader oxidative stress review notes that oxidative stress can be measured by lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, DNA damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction [N1-R2]. These markers are biologically relevant because they capture different downstream consequences of ROS/RNS excess: direct ROS detection, DNA/RNA damage, lipid damage, and vascular/inflammatory signaling [N6-R2][N6-R3][N4-F3][N1-R2].

How measurement context affects interpretation is a central limitation. The placental review explicitly states that OS biomarkers can vary with disease state and measurement setting, and that integrating OS biomarkers with other molecular and cellular markers offers improved potential for early identification of at-risk pregnancies [N4-F3]. This implies that a single biomarker may not reliably distinguish normal physiological OS from pathological OS, and that results can be influenced by gestational stage, placental location, disease severity, and assay conditions [N4-F3]. The human infertility literature also suggests that oxidative stress is associated with decreased fertility, but that the evidence is mostly derived from animal and in vitro studies, with limited direct human evidence [N5-R1]. This points to a general problem: many biomarker studies are observational or experimental rather than prospective human validation studies [N5-R1][N4-F3].

What measurement gaps exist in reproductive tissues is also clear. The placental review notes that clinical translation remains challenging and that future research should focus on validating biomarkers in large-scale studies [N4-F3]. It also highlights that promising biomarkers such as malondialdehyde, 8-isoprostane, and the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio have not yet been fully validated in clinical practice [N4-F3]. The broader oxidative stress review emphasizes that future randomized controlled clinical trials on humans are necessary to elucidate mechanisms and test antioxidant benefits [N1-F1]. In reproductive tissues, the evidence suggests gaps in tissue-specific biomarker validation, standardization of measurement protocols, and direct human evidence [N4-F3][N5-R1][N1-F1]. Another gap is that many biomarkers reflect cumulative or downstream damage rather than real-time redox status, which limits their utility for early intervention [N4-F3][N1-R2].

## Integrated explanation of how oxidative stress contributes to reproductive damage in females

Oxidative stress contributes to reproductive damage in females by disrupting multiple layers of reproductive biology, from tissue homeostasis and cell signaling to fertility outcomes and pregnancy success. The evidence across the branch reports points to a common mechanism: when reactive oxygen species (ROS) production exceeds antioxidant defenses, ROS overload damages cells, proteins, DNA, and mitochondria while also triggering inflammation and remodeling. This damage is not uniform across the female reproductive tract; instead, the most vulnerable tissues are the ovary, endometrium, and placenta, each with distinct but overlapping pathways connecting oxidative stress to reproductive dysfunction [N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-F3].

### 1) Which reproductive tissues are most vulnerable to oxidative stress?

The evidence is clearest for three main tissues: the ovarian follicle and granulosa cells, the endometrium, and the placenta.

- **Ovarian tissues** are especially vulnerable because oxidative stress accelerates ovarian aging by promoting apoptosis, inflammation, mitochondrial damage, telomere shortening, and biomacromolecular damage [N2-F2]. Granulosa cell apoptosis is a key factor in abnormal egg development and follicular atresia [N2-R2]. This makes the ovary particularly susceptible to damage during follicle development and ovulation [N2-F2].
- **Endometrium** is vulnerable because decidualization and implantation are highly sensitive to oxidative stress and related signaling disturbances [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Decidualization is also linked to endometrial receptivity, and dysregulation of this process can condition endometrial receptivity and contribute to pregnancy failure [N3-R2]. The branch report also notes that aberrant decidualization can lead to recurrent pregnancy loss and repeated implantation failure [N3-R3].
- **Placenta** is vulnerable because oxidative stress can disrupt trophoblast invasion, spiral artery remodeling, and placental perfusion, with direct consequences for pregnancy outcomes [N4-F3]. The placental review explicitly states that oxidative stress contributes to both normal and abnormal placentation and is implicated in miscarriage, preeclampsia, and intrauterine growth restriction [N4-F3].

In other words, oxidative stress damages the reproductive tract where the tissue is metabolically active, hormonally responsive, and involved in differentiation and immune/tissue remodeling [N1-R2][N2-F2][N4-F3].

### 2) How reactive oxygen species alter cell signaling and DNA/RNA

ROS do not simply cause random damage; they actively alter cell signaling and DNA/RNA biology in ways that can disrupt reproductive physiology.

- **Cell signaling** is altered through multiple pathways. In the ovary, ROS are involved in regulating oocyte growth, meiosis, ovulation, and follicular development [N2-F2]. ROS also regulate meiotic arrest and recovery, while antioxidant control dominates the progression of meiosis II [N2-F2]. In the placenta, ROS/RNS can damage lipids, proteins, and DNA, disrupt cellular functions, and trigger apoptosis and autophagy [N4-F3]. These effects suggest that ROS act as second messengers or as signals that shift the balance between cell survival and death [N2-F2][N4-F3].
- **DNA/RNA damage** is a major downstream consequence. The evidence explicitly states that oxidative stress can lead to DNA damage, and that 8-OHdG and other markers are used to measure DNA/RNA damage in oxidative stress contexts [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The broader oxidative stress review also notes that oxidative stress can trigger lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, DNA damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction [N1-R2]. In placental tissues, ROS/RNS can similarly damage DNA and disrupt cellular functions [N4-F3].

Taken together, ROS alter reproductive biology by changing signaling networks and damaging genetic material. This can impair follicle development, oocyte quality, implantation, and placental function [N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-F3].

### 3) What inflammatory and fibrotic changes follow oxidative stress

Oxidative stress does not simply cause direct molecular damage; it also triggers inflammatory and fibrotic-like changes that further compromise reproductive tissues.

- In the **ovary**, oxidative stress promotes apoptosis and inflammation, which together accelerate ovarian aging [N2-F2]. These changes contribute to reduced follicle number and quality, and to disorders such as diminished ovarian reserve, premature ovarian insufficiency, and poor ovarian response [N2-F2].
- In the **endometrium**, oxidative stress is associated with altered decidualization and ER stress, which condition endometrial receptivity [N3-R2]. Dysregulated decidualization can lead to implantation failure and pregnancy loss [N3-R3].
- In the **placenta**, oxidative stress impairs trophoblast function, inhibits EVT invasion, and disrupts spiral artery remodeling, leading to placental dysfunction and complications such as preeclampsia and intrauterine growth restriction [N4-F3]. Inflammation is a central theme: ROS can drive inflammatory precursors, and oxidative stress can trigger apoptosis and autophagy [N4-F3].

The fibrotic-like changes are indirect but important. The evidence points to tissue remodeling, loss of normal architecture, and loss of granulosa cells in the ovary [N2-R2][N2-F2]. In the endometrium, decidualization failure implies loss of the normal tissue state needed for implantation [N3-R2][N3-R3]. In the placenta, impaired remodeling and trophoblast function reflect a breakdown of tissue homeostasis rather than simple inflammation alone [N4-F3]. So, oxidative stress contributes to reproductive damage by creating a cascade of inflammation, cell death, and tissue remodeling [N1-R2][N2-F2][N4-F3].

### 4) How oxidative stress relates to reproductive outcomes

Oxidative stress is strongly linked to several reproductive outcomes, including ovulatory dysfunction, anovulation, early pregnancy loss, and implantation failure.

- **Ovulatory dysfunction and anovulation**: Oxidative stress accelerates ovarian aging and impairs follicle development by promoting granulosa cell apoptosis and follicular atresia [N2-R2][N2-F2]. It is also linked to diminished ovarian reserve, premature ovarian insufficiency, poor ovarian response, PCOS, endometriosis, and unexplained infertility [N1-F1][N2-F2]. These conditions all point to oxidative stress as a driver of reduced fertility and ovulatory failure [N2-F2][N1-F1].
- **Early pregnancy loss and implantation failure**: Oxidative stress affects implantation and decidualization. Dysregulation of decidualization due to ER stress and UPR conditions endometrial receptivity [N3-R2], and aberrant decidualization leads to recurrent pregnancy loss and repeated implantation failure [N3-R3]. In the placenta, oxidative stress contributes to both normal and abnormal placentation and is implicated in miscarriage, preeclampsia, and intrauterine growth restriction [N4-F3]. The placental review also notes that altered oxidant-antioxidant balance can trigger oxidative stress in the human placenta and is implicated in the etiology of recurrent pregnancy loss [N4-R4]. Oxidative stress biomarkers are strongly associated with disease progression and recurrent pregnancy loss [N4-R3].
- **Biomarkers used to measure oxidative stress in reproductive health**: The evidence supports several markers. ROS is proposed as a direct marker of oxidative stress [N6-R2][N6-R3]. 8-OHdG is proposed as a marker of DNA/RNA damage [N6-R2][N6-R3]. MDA is proposed as a marker of lipid peroxidation [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The placental review adds malondialdehyde, 8-isoprostane, and the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio as promising OS biomarkers [N4-F3]. The broader oxidative stress review notes that oxidative stress can be measured by lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, DNA damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction [N1-R2]. These biomarkers are biologically relevant because they reflect different aspects of oxidative stress: ROS production, DNA/RNA damage, lipid damage, and vascular/inflammatory signaling [N6-R2][N6-R3][N4-F3][N1-R2].

### 5) Biomarker interpretation and measurement limitations

The biomarker evidence is useful but limited. ROS, 8-OHdG, MDA, and other markers are important because they capture different downstream consequences of oxidative stress [N6-R2][N6-R3][N4-F3]. However, interpretation is context-dependent.

- **Measurement context affects interpretation**: The placental review explicitly states that OS biomarkers can vary with disease state and measurement setting, and that integrating OS biomarkers with other molecular and cellular markers improves the potential for early identification of at-risk pregnancies [N4-F3]. This means a single biomarker may not reliably distinguish normal physiological OS from pathological OS.
- **Measurement gaps exist in reproductive tissues**: The evidence suggests gaps in tissue-specific biomarker validation, standardization of measurement protocols, and direct human evidence [N4-F3][N5-R1][N1-F1]. The human infertility literature also notes that oxidative stress is associated with decreased fertility, but that the evidence is mostly derived from animal and in vitro studies, with limited direct human evidence [N5-R1]. The broader oxidative stress review emphasizes that future randomized controlled clinical trials on humans are necessary to elucidate mechanisms and test antioxidant benefits [N1-F1].

### 6) Clinical and translational context for treating oxidative stress in female reproduction

Antioxidant interventions are the most common proposed treatment, but the evidence is cautious.

- **Common antioxidant interventions and their reported effects on fertility**: The ovarian aging review notes that antioxidant supplementation can improve the ovarian OS state and enhance ovarian function [N2-F2]. It also reviews antioxidant therapies such as melatonin, vitamins, stem cell therapies, antioxidant monomers, and Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), but the evidence base is largely experimental [N2-F2]. Evidence on how oxidative stress causes direct tissue damage in the female reproductive tract

Oxidative stress is most directly damaging to reproductive tissues where ROS generation is tightly coupled to physiological function and where antioxidant defenses are relatively limited or overwhelmed. The strongest evidence points to ovarian tissues, endometrium, and placental tissues as especially vulnerable. In the ovary, oxidative stress accelerates ovarian aging by promoting apoptosis, inflammation, mitochondrial damage, telomere shortening, and biomacromolecular damage [N2-F2]. This includes granulosa cell apoptosis, which is central to abnormal egg development and follicular atresia [N2-R2]. In the endometrium, oxidative stress is tied to decidualization and implantation, with evidence that resistance to oxidative stress is necessary for successful trophoblast invasion and tissue integrity [N3-R1]. Decidualization is also linked to endometrial receptivity, and dysregulation of this process can condition endometrial receptivity and contribute to pregnancy failure [N3-R2]. The placenta likewise shows that oxidative stress can be both physiological and pathological, with placental dysfunction and pregnancy complications such as miscarriage, preeclampsia, and intrauterine growth restriction arising from an imbalance between oxidants and antioxidants [N4-F3].

Reactive oxygen species alter cell signaling and DNA/RNA through multiple pathways. ROS can disrupt normal physiological signaling by acting as second messengers or by modifying signaling molecules. In the ovary, ROS are involved in the regulation of oocyte growth, meiosis, ovulation, and follicular development [N2-F2]. ROS also regulate meiotic arrest and recovery, while antioxidant control dominates the progression of meiosis II [N2-F2]. At the same time, ROS can damage DNA/RNA. The evidence explicitly states that oxidative stress can lead to DNA damage, and that 8-OHdG and other markers are used to measure DNA/RNA damage in oxidative stress contexts [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The broader review also notes that oxidative stress can trigger lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, DNA damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction [N1-R2]. In placental tissues, ROS/RNS can damage lipids, proteins, and DNA, disrupt cellular functions, and trigger apoptosis and autophagy [N4-F3]. These effects are not limited to direct DNA damage; ROS can also interfere with gene expression and signaling by modifying key proteins and metabolic pathways.

Inflammatory and fibrotic changes follow oxidative stress through a cascade of signaling and tissue responses. In the ovary, oxidative stress promotes apoptosis and inflammation, which together accelerate ovarian aging [N2-F2]. In the endometrium, oxidative stress is associated with altered decidualization and ER stress, which condition endometrial receptivity [N3-R2]. The placenta shows that oxidative stress can impair trophoblast function, inhibit EVT invasion, and disrupt spiral artery remodeling, leading to placental dysfunction and complications like preeclampsia and intrauterine growth restriction [N4-F3]. Inflammation is a central theme: ROS can drive inflammatory precursors, and oxidative stress can trigger cell death pathways such as apoptosis and autophagy [N4-F3]. Fibrotic-like changes are implied indirectly through tissue remodeling and loss of normal architecture, including granulosa cell loss and follicular atresia [N2-R2][N2-F2]. Taken together, oxidative stress does not merely cause localized DNA/RNA damage; it reshapes tissue homeostasis through inflammation, apoptosis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and remodeling [N1-R2][N2-F2][N4-F3].

Which tissues are most vulnerable? The ovarian follicle and granulosa cells are especially vulnerable because oxidative stress promotes apoptosis and follicular atresia [N2-R2][N2-F2]. The endometrium is vulnerable because decidualization and implantation are highly sensitive to oxidative stress and related signaling disturbances [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The placenta is vulnerable because oxidative stress can disrupt trophoblast invasion, spiral artery remodeling, and placental perfusion, with direct consequences for pregnancy outcomes [N4-F3]. These tissues share a common vulnerability: they are sites of active metabolism, differentiation, and immune/tissue remodeling, which make them especially sensitive to ROS overload and antioxidant deficiency [N1-R2][N2-F2][N4-F3].

Evidence on reproductive outcomes linked to oxidative stress

Oxidative stress is strongly linked to ovulatory dysfunction and anovulation through effects on ovarian function and follicle development. The ovarian aging review states that oxidative stress accelerates ovarian aging by promoting apoptosis, inflammation, mitochondrial damage, telomere shortening, and biomacromolecular damage [N2-F2]. It also notes that follicular fluid oxidative stress markers correlate with decreased embryo quality, and that oxidative stress contributes to the etiology of ovarian aging and other ovarian disorders [N2-R5]. In the ovary, oxidative stress impairs follicle development by promoting granulosa cell apoptosis and follicular atresia [N2-R2]. These effects are consistent with ovulatory dysfunction because they reduce follicle number and quality, disrupt steroid production, and compromise oocyte maturation [N2-F2]. The evidence also links oxidative stress to diminished ovarian reserve, premature ovarian insufficiency, and poor ovarian response, all of which are clinical manifestations of anovulation and reduced fertility [N2-F2]. In short, oxidative stress is not merely an incidental feature of ovarian aging; it is a driver of the structural and functional changes that underlie ovulatory failure [N2-F2][N2-R5].

Oxidative stress also plays a major role in early pregnancy loss and implantation failure. In the endometrium, oxidative stress affects decidualization and implantation receptivity. Dysregulation of the decidualization process due to ER stress and UPR conditions endometrial receptivity [N3-R2], and aberrant decidualization leads to pregnancy failures such as recurrent pregnancy loss and repeated implantation failure [N3-R3]. The placenta shows that oxidative stress contributes to both normal and abnormal placentation and is implicated in miscarriage, preeclampsia, and intrauterine growth restriction [N4-F3]. The placental review explicitly states that altered balance between oxidants and antioxidants can trigger oxidative stress in human placenta and has important implications in the etiology of recurrent pregnancy loss [N4-R4]. It also notes that oxidative stress biomarkers are strongly associated with disease progression and recurrent pregnancy loss [N4-R3]. These findings point to oxidative stress as a key contributor to early pregnancy failure by impairing implantation, decidualization, placental development, and trophoblast function [N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-F3][N4-R4].

As for biomarkers used to measure oxidative stress in reproductive health, the evidence supports a small set of well-established markers. ROS itself is proposed as a direct marker of oxidative stress [N6-R2][N6-R3]. 8-OHdG is proposed as a marker of DNA/RNA damage [N6-R2][N6-R3]. Malondialdehyde (MDA) is proposed as a marker of lipid peroxidation [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The placental review also highlights malondialdehyde, 8-isoprostane, and the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio as promising OS biomarkers [N4-F3]. The broader reproductive literature also notes that oxidative stress can be measured by lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, DNA damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction [N1-R2]. These markers are biologically relevant because they reflect different aspects of oxidative stress: ROS production, DNA/RNA damage, lipid damage, and inflammatory or vascular signaling [N6-R2][N6-R3][N4-F3]. However, the evidence also suggests that these markers are not interchangeable or universally applicable across tissues. In reproductive tissues, the placental review emphasizes that biomarker interpretation is context-dependent and that OS biomarkers can vary with disease state and measurement setting [N4-F3]. The human infertility literature similarly indicates that oxidative stress is associated with decreased fertility, but that the evidence is mostly derived from animal and in vitro studies, with limited direct human evidence [N5-R1].

## Integrated explanation of how oxidative stress contributes to reproductive damage in females

Oxidative stress contributes to reproductive damage in females by disrupting multiple layers of reproductive biology, from tissue homeostasis and cell signaling to fertility outcomes and pregnancy success. The evidence across the branch reports points to a common mechanism: when reactive oxygen species (ROS) production exceeds antioxidant defenses, ROS overload damages cells, proteins, DNA, and mitochondria while also triggering inflammation and remodeling. This damage is not uniform across the female reproductive tract; instead, the most vulnerable tissues are the ovary, endometrium, and placenta, each with distinct but overlapping pathways connecting oxidative stress to reproductive dysfunction [N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-F3].

### 1) Which reproductive tissues are most vulnerable to oxidative stress?

The evidence is clearest for three main tissues: the ovarian follicle and granulosa cells, the endometrium, and the placenta.

- **Ovarian tissues** are especially vulnerable because oxidative stress accelerates ovarian aging by promoting apoptosis, inflammation, mitochondrial damage, telomere shortening, and biomacromolecular damage [N2-F2]. Granulosa cell apoptosis is a key factor in abnormal egg development and follicular atresia [N2-R2]. This makes the ovary particularly susceptible to damage during follicle development and ovulation [N2-F2].
- **Endometrium** is vulnerable because decidualization and implantation are highly sensitive to oxidative stress and related signaling disturbances [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Oxidative stress contributes to reproductive damage in females by damaging the most metabolically and hormonally active reproductive tissues—the ovary, endometrium, and placenta—through ROS overload, DNA/RNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, apoptosis, inflammation, and tissue remodeling [N1-R2][N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-F3]. ## Integrated explanation of how oxidative stress contributes to reproductive damage in females

Oxidative stress contributes to reproductive damage in females by disrupting multiple layers of reproductive biology, from tissue homeostasis and cell signaling to fertility outcomes and pregnancy success. The evidence across the branch reports points to a common mechanism: when reactive oxygen species (ROS) production exceeds antioxidant defenses, ROS overload damages cells, proteins, DNA, and mitochondria while also triggering inflammation and remodeling. This damage is not uniform across the female reproductive tract; instead, the most vulnerable tissues are the ovary, endometrium, and placenta, each with distinct but overlapping pathways connecting oxidative stress to reproductive dysfunction [N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-F3].

### 1) Which reproductive tissues are most vulnerable to oxidative stress?

The evidence is clearest for three main tissues: the ovarian follicle and granulosa cells, the endometrium, and the placenta.

- **Ovarian tissues** are especially vulnerable because oxidative stress accelerates ovarian aging by promoting apoptosis, inflammation, mitochondrial damage, telomere shortening, and biomacromolecular damage [N2-F2]. Granulosa cell apoptosis is a key factor in abnormal egg development and follicular atresia [N2-R2]. This makes the ovary particularly susceptible to damage during follicle development and ovulation [N2-F2].
- **Endometrium** is vulnerable because decidualization and implantation are highly sensitive to oxidative stress and related signaling disturbances [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Decidualization is also linked to endometrial receptivity, and dysregulation of this process can condition endometrial receptivity and contribute to pregnancy failure [N3-R2]. The branch report also notes that aberrant decidualization can lead to recurrent pregnancy loss and repeated implantation failure [N3-R3].
- **Placenta** is vulnerable because oxidative stress can disrupt trophoblast invasion, spiral artery remodeling, and placental perfusion, with direct consequences for pregnancy outcomes [N4-F3]. The placental review explicitly states that oxidative stress contributes to both normal and abnormal placentation and is implicated in miscarriage, preeclampsia, and intrauterine growth restriction [N4-F3].

In other words, oxidative stress damages the reproductive tract where the tissue is metabolically active, hormonally responsive, and involved in differentiation and immune/tissue remodeling [N1-R2][N2-F2][N4-F3].

### 2) How reactive oxygen species alter cell signaling and DNA/RNA

ROS do not simply cause random damage; they actively alter cell signaling and DNA/RNA biology in ways that can disrupt reproductive physiology.

- **Cell signaling** is altered through multiple pathways. In the ovary, ROS are involved in regulating oocyte growth, meiosis, ovulation, and follicular development [N2-F2]. ROS also regulate meiotic arrest and recovery, while antioxidant control dominates the progression of meiosis II [N2-F2]. In the placenta, ROS/RNS can damage lipids, proteins, and DNA, disrupt cellular functions, and trigger apoptosis and autophagy [N4-F3]. These effects suggest that ROS act as second messengers or as signals that shift the balance between cell survival and death [N2-F2][N4-F3].
- **DNA/RNA damage** is a major downstream consequence. The evidence explicitly states that oxidative stress can lead to DNA damage, and that 8-OHdG and other markers are used to measure DNA/RNA damage in oxidative stress contexts [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The broader oxidative stress review also notes that oxidative stress can trigger lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, DNA damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction [N1-R2]. In placental tissues, ROS/RNS can similarly damage DNA and disrupt cellular functions [N4-F3].

Taken together, ROS alter reproductive biology by changing signaling networks and damaging genetic material. This can impair follicle development, oocyte quality, implantation, and placental function [N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-F3].

### 3) What inflammatory and fibrotic changes follow oxidative stress

Oxidative stress does not simply cause direct molecular damage; it also triggers inflammatory and fibrotic-like changes that further compromise reproductive tissues.

- In the **ovary**, oxidative stress promotes apoptosis and inflammation, which together accelerate ovarian aging [N2-F2]. These changes contribute to reduced follicle number and quality, and to disorders such as diminished ovarian reserve, premature ovarian insufficiency, and poor ovarian response [N2-F2].
- In the **endometrium**, oxidative stress is associated with altered decidualization and ER stress, which condition endometrial receptivity [N3-R2]. Dysregulated decidualization can lead to implantation failure and pregnancy loss [N3-R3].
- In the **placenta**, oxidative stress impairs trophoblast function, inhibits EVT invasion, and disrupts spiral artery remodeling, leading to placental dysfunction and complications such as preeclampsia and intrauterine growth restriction [N4-F3]. Inflammation is a central theme: ROS can drive inflammatory precursors, and oxidative stress can trigger apoptosis and autophagy [N4-F3].

The fibrotic-like changes are indirect but important. The evidence points to tissue remodeling, loss of normal architecture, and loss of granulosa cells in the ovary [N2-R2][N2-F2]. In the endometrium, decidualization failure implies loss of the normal tissue state needed for implantation [N3-R2][N3-R3]. In the placenta, impaired remodeling and trophoblast function reflect a breakdown of tissue homeostasis rather than simple inflammation alone [N4-F3]. So, oxidative stress contributes to reproductive damage by creating a cascade of inflammation, cell death, and tissue remodeling [N1-R2][N2-F2][N4-F3].

### 4) How oxidative stress relates to reproductive outcomes

Oxidative stress is strongly linked to several reproductive outcomes, including ovulatory dysfunction, anovulation, early pregnancy loss, and implantation failure.

- **Ovulatory dysfunction and anovulation**: Oxidative stress accelerates ovarian aging and impairs follicle development by promoting granulosa cell apoptosis and follicular atresia [N2-R2][N2-F2]. It is also linked to diminished ovarian reserve, premature ovarian insufficiency, poor ovarian response, PCOS, endometriosis, and unexplained infertility [N1-F1][N2-F2]. These conditions all point to oxidative stress as a driver of reduced fertility and ovulatory failure [N2-F2][N1-F1].
- **Early pregnancy loss and implantation failure**: Oxidative stress affects implantation and decidualization. Dysregulation of decidualization due to ER stress and UPR conditions endometrial receptivity [N3-R2], and aberrant decidualization leads to recurrent pregnancy loss and repeated implantation failure [N3-R3]. In the placenta, oxidative stress contributes to both normal and abnormal placentation and is implicated in miscarriage, preeclampsia, and intrauterine growth restriction [N4-F3]. The placental review also notes that altered oxidant-antioxidant balance can trigger oxidative stress in the human placenta and is implicated in the etiology of recurrent pregnancy loss [N4-R4]. Oxidative stress biomarkers are strongly associated with disease progression and recurrent pregnancy loss [N4-R3].
- **Biomarkers used to measure oxidative stress in reproductive health**: The evidence supports several markers. ROS is proposed as a direct marker of oxidative stress [N6-R2][N6-R3]. 8-OHdG is proposed as a marker of DNA/RNA damage [N6-R2][N6-R3]. MDA is proposed as a marker of lipid peroxidation [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The placental review adds malondialdehyde, 8-isoprostane, and the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio as promising OS biomarkers [N4-F3]. The broader oxidative stress review notes that oxidative stress can be measured by lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, DNA damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction [N1-R2]. These biomarkers are biologically relevant because they reflect different aspects of oxidative stress: ROS production, DNA/RNA damage, lipid damage, and vascular/inflammatory signaling [N6-R2][N6-R3][N4-F3][N1-R2].

### 5) Biomarker interpretation and measurement limitations

The biomarker evidence is useful but limited. ROS, 8-OHdG, MDA, and other markers are important because they capture different downstream consequences of oxidative stress [N6-R2][N6-R3][N4-F3]. However, interpretation is context-dependent.

- **Measurement context affects interpretation**: The placental review explicitly states that OS biomarkers can vary with disease state and measurement setting, and that integrating OS biomarkers with other molecular and cellular markers improves the potential for early identification of at-risk pregnancies [N4-F3]. This means a single biomarker may not reliably distinguish normal physiological OS from pathological OS.
- **Measurement gaps exist in reproductive tissues**: The evidence suggests gaps in tissue-specific biomarker validation, standardization of measurement protocols, and direct human evidence [N4-F3][N5-R1][N1-F1]. The human infertility literature also notes that oxidative stress is associated with decreased fertility, but that the evidence is mostly derived from animal and in vitro studies, with limited direct human evidence [N5-R1]. The broader oxidative stress review emphasizes that future randomized controlled clinical trials on humans are necessary to elucidate mechanisms and test antioxidant benefits [N1-F1].

### 6) Clinical and translational context for treating oxidative stress in female reproduction

Antioxidant interventions are the most common proposed treatment, but the evidence is cautious.

- **Common antioxidant interventions and their reported effects on fertility**: The ovarian aging review notes that antioxidant supplementation can improve the ovarian OS state and enhance ovarian function [N2-F2]. It also reviews antioxidant therapies such as melatonin, vitamins, stem cell therapies, antioxidant monomers, and Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), but the evidence base is largely experimental [N2-F2]. The broader oxidative stress review states that antioxidant supplementation may be effective in controlling ROS production and continues to be explored as a potential strategy to overcome reproductive disorders associated with infertility [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that antioxidant supplementation of ART culture media is of interest for improving ART success [N1-F1].
- **Limitations and gaps in human evidence**: The ovarian aging review explicitly states that investigations conducted to date have been through animal or in vitro studies, which have produced largely conflicting results [N2-F2]. The human female infertility review likewise notes that no studies to date have directly assessed the relationship in humans [N5-R1]. The oxidative stress review further emphasizes that future randomized controlled clinical trials on humans are necessary to elucidate the precise mechanisms through which OS affects female reproductive abilities [N1-F1]. These limitations suggest that human evidence remains sparse, heterogeneous, and mostly indirect [N5-R1][N1-F1].
- **How oxidative stress fits into broader reproductive disease mechanisms**: Oxidative stress is not an isolated phenomenon. It is embedded in the pathogenesis of several reproductive diseases and pregnancy complications. In the ovary, it is linked to ovarian aging, diminished ovarian reserve, premature ovarian insufficiency, poor ovarian response, PCOS, endometriosis, and unexplained infertility [N1-F1][N2-F2]. In the endometrium, it is linked to implantation failure and recurrent pregnancy loss [N3-R2][N3-R3]. In the placenta, it is linked to preeclampsia, intrauterine growth restriction, and miscarriage [N4-F3]. The broader reproductive literature also ties oxidative stress to lifestyle factors, environmental pollutants, obesity, malnutrition, cigarette smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs, and occupational exposures [N1-F1]. This places oxidative stress within a broader pathogenic framework in which reproductive dysfunction arises from metabolic, inflammatory, hormonal, and environmental insults that all contribute to ROS imbalance [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

### 7) Bottom line

Oxidative stress contributes to reproductive damage in females by damaging the most metabolically and hormonally active reproductive tissues—the ovary, endometrium, and placenta—through ROS overload, DNA/RNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, apoptosis, inflammation, and tissue remodeling [N1-R2][N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-F3]. It is linked to ovulatory dysfunction, anovulation, implantation failure, and early pregnancy loss, and the most important biomarkers include ROS, 8-OHdG, MDA, and placental-specific markers such as sFlt-1/PlGF [N6-R2][N6-R3][N4-F3]. However, the evidence is still mostly indirect and limited in humans, so antioxidant interventions remain promising but not yet firmly established as a standard treatment [N2-F2][N5-R1][N1-F1]. Overall, oxidative stress is a central player in reproductive disease, but its effects are best understood as part of a larger network of metabolic, inflammatory, and environmental factors that shape reproductive health [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].
